question: lamontae wants approval ratings in the game in some form. Answer nationwide, as one set, for officeholders at every level: president; members of Congress and Congress as a body; governors; state legislators and legislatures; mayors, county executives and council members. (1) Measurement: who actually measures and publishes approval at each level (national pollsters, state university polls, local media polls), how often, with what sample sizes and margins, and at which levels no regular polling exists at all, so the game knows where a number is observed and where it is only inferred. (2) Baselines: typical levels and spreads at each level (for example, how governors compare with state legislatures, and members' own approval versus their chamber's), honeymoon effects, and how approval typically drifts across a term. (3) What moves it and how fast: scandal (by type and severity, and how long the effect lasts), the local and national economy (unemployment, inflation, gas prices), passing or failing legislation, disasters and crisis response, party and national mood, and press coverage volume and tone; give effect sizes and decay rates from studies where they exist. (4) Consequences: how approval relates to re-election odds, primary challenges, retirement decisions, legislative bargaining power (including a legislature's willingness to override a veto), party support, recall where a state allows it, and donor or endorsement behavior. (5) Private versus public: how an officeholder's standing with colleagues, donors and party differs from their public approval. Mark each figure as measured, synthesized or assumed, and say where no evidence exists.

title: How approval of officeholders is measured, what moves it, and what it does
usableAnswer: A table by level of office: who measures approval, how often, typical level and spread, and how approval maps to re-election odds; a table of drivers with effect size, onset and decay, and their sources; the levels where no polling exists, with a stated fallback for inferring approval there; and each figure marked measured, synthesized or assumed.
whyItMatters: The game has no approval rating of any kind. The only public-opinion measure is a candidate's campaign support share, which exists only during a campaign (src/simulation/campaigns.ts and campaign-support.ts at main 616dcdb5). src/simulation/service-delivery-response.ts states that delivered service changes no approval rating because none exists. So a scandal, a law or a bad economy cannot change how the public sees a sitting officeholder between elections, and lamontae asked, after following a scandal in playtest, whether it cost her anything beyond coverage. The corrupt-life playtest shows the gap: Lucia Moran, Governor of Alaska in play, had a public finding for taking campaign money, vetoed all three bills sent to her in year one, froze spending and let a disaster pass without asking for federal help, and nothing anywhere records how the public feels about her.

answer.summary: Owner decision (2026-09-22): show a numeric approval percentage to the player only when an in-world poll actually measured it; where no poll exists people still hold opinions and act on them, shown through behavior, conversations, reporting and election results, and the game's latent public attitudes stay separate from any observed poll. Measurement by level: the president has the longest series (Gallup since 1938, cadence and mode changed over time; Morning Consult monthly state estimates from a rolling three-month pool of over 250,000 registered voters, state margins from about 1 to 6 points). Congress as a body: Gallup since 1974; body approval says nothing about any one member. Senators and governors: Morning Consult tracks all 100 senators and 50 governors the same way; state and university polls add periodic readings (PPIC California, September 2026, 1,745 adults, plus or minus 3). State legislature as a body, individual legislators, mayors, county officials and council members: only occasional local or sponsor-specific polls, no national series, so the national baseline is UNKNOWN, not neutral or zero. Rules: approval is not favorability and not vote share; keep wording, population, dates, mode, sample, weighting and margin with every number; report don't-know separately; suppress or mark unknown when a sample cannot support a small-area estimate. Drivers: only documented associations, not coefficients: rally effects after some security crises, which have become rarer; economic perceptions mattered in one Clinton case; no systematic Dow-to-approval link. Suggested shape: a simulation-private estimate per office and jurisdiction (approve, disapprove, unsure, with uncertainty and recency), responding probabilistically to recorded events, kept separate from election results and favorability.
answer.stillOpen: No validated effect sizes, onset or decay for any driver, and no mapping from approval to re-election odds. No national starting value for any state or local office; those are UNKNOWN.
